question: Why does Twitter use a hybrid approach combining write fan-out and read-side merging for user timelines?
reference_answer: For most users, tweets are fanned out into followers' home timeline caches at write time. For celebrities with a very large number of followers, fan-out would mean an enormous number of writes, so their tweets are fetched separately and merged into the timeline when it is read.

question: 2PC vs 3PC
reference_answer: Two-phase commit (2PC) guarantees atomic commit but is a blocking protocol: it can get stuck waiting for the coordinator to recover. Three-phase commit (3PC) is a proposed nonblocking alternative, but it assumes a network with bounded delay and nodes with bounded response times, which most real systems cannot guarantee.
notes: orig id 8. Original page 355 is printed (PDF 377); the comparison is printed 358-359 (PDF 380-381). Reference reworded to match the book: the original mentioned atomic broadcast, which this passage does not.

question: A storage engine keeps its data files sorted by key. How does that let it find a key without holding every key in memory?
reference_answer: It can use a sparse in-memory index: one key for every few kilobytes of segment file is sufficient, because a few kilobytes can be scanned very quickly.
evidence_terms: one key for every few kilobytes
notes: From agent batch 2, orig id 9. Question rewritten: the original contained the phrase sparse in-memory index (keyword leakage). Reference answer reworded to the book; the original said one key per block of disk.

question: Why does a B-tree write each piece of data to disk more than once?
reference_answer: A B-tree index must write every piece of data at least twice: once to the write-ahead log and once to the tree page itself. There is also overhead from writing an entire page at a time even if only a few bytes changed.
notes: From agent batch 2, orig id 10. Question rewritten: the original asked for the cause of write amplification in B-trees, but the book uses that term for log-structured indexes on this page. The 4 KB figure in the original answer is not in the text.

question: A client holds a lock, pauses for a long time, then writes to storage after its lock has expired. How can the storage service protect itself from that stale write?
reference_answer: Every time the lock server grants a lock or lease it also returns a fencing token, a number that increases every time a lock is granted. The storage service rejects a write carrying a token older than one it has already processed.
notes: From agent batch 2, orig id 11. Question rewritten: the original contained the term fencing tokens.

question: What is the key timing property that distinguishes linearizability from eventual consistency?
reference_answer: Linearizability is a recency guarantee: the value read is the most recent, up-to-date value, not one from a stale cache or replica.
notes: From agent batch 2, orig id 12.

question: What is the difference between checking data structure when reading versus checking structure when writing in document stores?
reference_answer: Schema-on-read means the structure of the data is implicit and only interpreted when the data is read. Schema-on-write is the traditional relational approach where the schema is explicit and the database ensures all written data conforms to it.
notes: From agent batch 2, orig id 13. Good paraphrase: the question avoids both terms.

question: Why do log-structured storage engines use probabilistic set membership structures for key lookups?
reference_answer: Looking up a key that does not exist is slow because the memtable and every segment back to the oldest must be checked. A Bloom filter is a memory-efficient structure for approximating the contents of a set; it can tell you a key does not appear and saves unnecessary disk reads.
notes: From agent batch 2, orig id 14. Good paraphrase: the question avoids the term Bloom filter.

question: How can an application be built by composing specialized storage and processing systems around dataflow, instead of relying on one monolithic database?

question: What happens when a leaderless database accepts writes on reachable nodes outside a key's designated home nodes during a network outage?
reference_answer: It uses a sloppy quorum: writes are accepted on reachable nodes that are not among the designated home nodes, and once the interruption is fixed, hinted handoff sends those writes to the home nodes.
notes: From agent batch 2, orig id 16. Both terms also co-occur on PDF 201, 206, 356 and in the index; check the chunk boundaries.

question: What are the trade-offs between LSM-trees and B-trees regarding write throughput versus read throughput?
reference_answer: LSM-trees are typically faster for writes, whereas B-trees are thought to be faster for reads. Reads are slower on LSM-trees because they have to check several data structures and SSTables at different stages of compaction.
evidence_terms: LSM-trees are typically faster for writes
notes: From agent batch 2, orig id 17. Original answer said B-trees are typically faster for reads; the book says thought to be.

question: How do document-partitioned (local) secondary indexes compare to term-partitioned (global) secondary indexes?
reference_answer: With document-partitioned indexes each partition maintains its own secondary index, so a read must query all partitions (scatter/gather). Term-partitioned indexes cover all data, so a read can go to one partition, but writes are slower and more complicated.
notes: From agent batch 2, orig id 18. Original gold page was the range 17-19 (invalid) and the term scatter-gather is not verbatim. Names both concepts in the question, so it favours keyword search.

question: How does a broadcast hash join differ from a reduce-side sort-merge join in MapReduce?
reference_answer: A broadcast hash join loads the small input entirely into a hash table in each mapper and scans the large input, with no sorting or reducer. A sort-merge join sorts and partitions both inputs by join key so matching keys reach the same reducer.
notes: From agent batch 2, orig id 19. Evidence is nine pages apart, so a chunker with small chunks must retrieve both places. Names both concepts in the question.

question: What is the operational difference between a stream-stream join and a stream-table join?
reference_answer: A stream-stream (window) join matches events from two streams within a time window. A stream-table join enriches a stream of events by looking up records in a table kept up to date.
notes: From agent batch 2, orig id 20. Original had no gold page. Names both concepts in the question.

question: How do transaction processing systems typically enforce that concurrent updates to the same database object do not overwrite uncommitted changes?
reference_answer: Databases most commonly prevent dirty writes by using row-level locks, requiring a transaction to acquire a lock on an object before modifying it.
evidence_terms: prevent dirty writes by using row-level locks
notes: From NotebookLM batch 3, orig n003. Source: "Most commonly, databases prevent dirty writes by using row-level locks: when a transaction wants to modify a particular object (row or document), it must first acquire a lock on that object." === PDF PAGE 258 (printed 236) ===

question: Why is it impossible to determine an ideal fixed duration for declaring a remote server dead over typical internet or cloud infrastructure?
reference_answer: Asynchronous networks exhibit unbounded delays with no upper bound on packet delivery times, and server request handling times are similarly variable, making any low fixed timeout vulnerable to false failure declarations during transient load spikes.
notes: From NotebookLM batch 3, orig n004. Source: "Unfortunately, most systems we work with have neither of those guarantees: asynchronous networks have unbounded delays (that is, they try to deliver packets as quickly as possible, but there is no upper limit on the time it may take for a packet to arrive), and most server implementations cannot guarantee that they can handle requests within some maximum time (see “Response time guarantees” on page 298)." === PDF PAGE 304 (printed 282) ===

question: What foundational assumption do most non-cryptographic distributed database algorithms make regarding the integrity of messages received from participating cluster nodes?
reference_answer: Distributed database systems generally assume nodes are unreliable but honest, meaning that while nodes may be slow or crash, any message sent accurately reflects the protocol rules rather than containing malicious or corrupted claims.
notes: From NotebookLM batch 3, orig n005. Source: "In this book we assume that nodes are unreliable but honest: they may be slow or never respond (due to a fault), and their state may be outdated (due to a GC pause or network delays), but we assume that if a node does respond, it is telling the “truth”: to the best of its knowledge, it is playing by the rules of the protocol." === PDF PAGE 326 (printed 304) ===

question: Why do leaderless replication systems that rely exclusively on client-side fixes during query execution risk reduced durability for infrequently accessed records?
reference_answer: Without a background anti-entropy process to continuously sync missing data between replicas, records that are rarely queried will not trigger read repair and may remain missing from stale nodes.
evidence_terms: read repair is only performed when a value is read
notes: From NotebookLM batch 3, orig n006. Source: "Note that without an anti-entropy process, values that are rarely read may be missing from some replicas and thus have reduced durability, because read repair is only performed when a value is read by the application." === PDF PAGE 201 (printed 179) ===

question: How do multi-leader architectures avoid inter-datacenter network latencies during updates, and what mathematical condition must quorum sizes satisfy in leaderless stores to guarantee reading an up-to-date value?
reference_answer: Multi-leader architectures avoid inter-datacenter write latencies by processing each write in the local datacenter and replicating it asynchronously. In leaderless replication, reading an up-to-date value requires that the sum of write confirmed nodes (w) and read queried nodes (r) is strictly greater than the total replica count (n), i.e., w + r > n.
notes: From NotebookLM batch 3, orig n007. Stapled question: two unrelated sub-questions joined with 'and', so a failure may be in either half. Source: "In a multi-leader configuration, every write can be processed in the local datacenter and is replicated asynchronously to the other datacenters. Thus, the inter-datacenter network delay is hidden from users..." === PDF PAGE 191 (printed 169) ===; "As long as w + r > n, we expect to get an up-to-date value when reading, because at least one of the r nodes we’re reading from must be up to date." === PDF PAGE 201 (printed 179) ===

question: How can single-leader systems ensure a user immediately sees their own edits, and why can relying on physical time-of-day timestamps cause data loss when ordering concurrent updates?
reference_answer: Single-leader systems can ensure read-after-write consistency for user edits by routing reads of user-modifiable data (such as a user's own profile) to the leader. Using physical time-of-day timestamps to order updates can silently drop newer writes if clock skew assigns an earlier timestamp to a causally later write.
evidence_terms: read the user’s own profile from the leader
notes: From NotebookLM batch 3, orig n008. Stapled question: two unrelated sub-questions joined with 'and', so a failure may be in either half. Source: "Thus, a simple rule is: always read the user’s own profile from the leader, and any other users’ profiles from a follower." === PDF PAGE 185 (printed 163) ===; "In effect, client B’s increment operation will be lost. This conflict resolution strategy is called last write wins (LWW)..." === PDF PAGE 314 (printed 292) ===

question: How do pessimistic concurrency control mechanisms and optimistic concurrency control mechanisms differ in their handling of conflicting transaction operations?
reference_answer: Pessimistic concurrency control blocks concurrent operations by holding locks until completion, whereas optimistic concurrency control allows transactions to execute without blocking and aborts them upon commit if serialization conflicts are detected.
notes: From NotebookLM batch 3, orig n009. Source: "However, if there is enough spare capacity, and if contention between transactions is not too high, optimistic concurrency control techniques tend to perform better than pessimistic ones." === PDF PAGE 284 (printed 262) ===

question: Why do stream processing systems avoid querying external databases across a network to enrich event logs, and what mechanism is used instead?
reference_answer: Querying a remote database for every event causes high network latency and risks overloading the database; instead, stream processors load a local copy of the database into memory or local disk to perform lookups locally.
evidence_terms: round-trip time to the database server
notes: From NotebookLM batch 4, orig n403. Genuine cross-reference: PDF 496 points back to the activity-events example at printed 404 (PDF 426). '...such remote queries are likely to be slow and risk overloading the database [75].' === PDF PAGE 426 (printed 404) === / === PDF PAGE 496 (printed 474) ===; 'Another approach is to load a copy of the database into the stream processor so that it can be queried locally without a network round-trip. This technique is very similar to the hash joins we discussed in “Map-Side Joins” on page 408: the local copy of the database might be an in-memory hash table if it is small enough, or an index on the local disk.' === PDF PAGE 496 (printed 474) ===

question: How does partitioning log message streams to a single consumer thread enable systems to enforce unique values without running distributed consensus algorithms?
reference_answer: By assigning an entire log partition to a single consumer thread and routing candidate requests by key hash, all requests for a given value arrive in a strict total order handled by one thread, which can deterministically approve the first request and reject duplicates.
notes: From NotebookLM batch 4, orig n404. Genuine cross-reference: PDF 544 points back to printed 448 (PDF 470). 'To achieve load balancing across a group of consumers, instead of assigning individual messages to consumer clients, the broker can assign entire partitions to nodes in the consumer group.' === PDF PAGE 470 (printed 448) ===; 'A stream processor consumes all the messages in a log partition sequentially on a single thread (see “Logs compared to traditional messaging” on page 448). Thus, if the log is partitioned based on the value that needs to be unique, a stream processor can unambiguously and deterministically decide which one of several conflicting operations came first.' === PDF PAGE 544 (printed 522) ===

question: How do query engines minimize CPU branch mispredictions and function call overhead when processing filtering conditions over columnar storage?
reference_answer: Query engines use vectorized processing to iterate through chunks of encoded column data in tight CPU loops without individual function calls or branch mispredictions for each record.
notes: From NotebookLM batch 4, orig n405. Redundant evidence: PDF 121 and PDF 450 each state the concept. Prefer hit@k over recall@k for this question. 'Query engines can take a chunk of compressed column data that fits in the CPU’s L1 cache, and iterate through it in a tight loop (that is, with no function calls). A CPU can execute such loops much faster than code with a lot of function calls and branch mispredictions. This is known as vectorized processing.' === PDF PAGE 121 (printed 99) ===; 'If such simple filtering and mapping operations are expressed in a declarative way, the query optimizer can take advantage of column-oriented storage layouts (see “Column-Oriented Storage” on page 95) and write tight loops that execute directly on chunks of encoded column data without function calls (known as vectorized processing [78]).' === PDF PAGE 450 (printed 428) ===

question: Why do APIs returning 64-bit integer identifiers in text payload structures provide the value as both a numeric field and a literal character string?
reference_answer: Because text-based data formats like JSON do not specify numeric precision or distinguish integers from floating-point numbers, integers exceeding 2^53 lose accuracy when parsed by environments that use double-precision floating-point arithmetic.
notes: From NotebookLM batch 4, orig n406. 'This is a problem when dealing with large numbers; for example, integers greater than 2^53 cannot be exactly represented in an IEEE 754 double-precision floating-point number, so such numbers become inaccurate when parsed in a language that uses floating-point numbers (such as JavaScript).' === PDF PAGE 136 (printed 114) ===

question: Why does sorting records scale better to datasets exceeding available system RAM than accumulating occurrence counts in memory data structures?
reference_answer: In-memory hash tables require random memory access proportional to the number of distinct keys, running out of RAM when the working set is large, whereas sorting algorithms spill data to disk and process segment files using sequential disk I/O.
notes: From NotebookLM batch 4, orig n407. 'If this working set is small enough, an in-memory hash table works fine—even on a laptop. On the other hand, if the job’s working set is larger than the available memory, the sorting approach has the advantage that it can make efficient use of disks.' === PDF PAGE 415 (printed 393) ===
